title: A boundary map: boundary types, disputes and the law of the sea zones

readings.title: Three land boundaries and one sea

parts.label: A
parts.demand: Give the information asked for: a word or short phrase can earn the point, with no reasons needed.
parts.prompt: Identify the type of boundary at A.
parts.sample: The boundary at A is a geometric boundary: it follows the 49th parallel, a line of latitude, between the United States and Canada.

parts.label: B
parts.demand: Give the relevant characteristics: what it is like, where and how much. A name alone earns nothing.
parts.prompt: Describe how the boundary at B works.

rubric.point: Describes the Korean demilitarized zone as a closed boundary: a strip with no armed forces, fenced and guarded, that stops almost all crossing.
accept: a demilitarized zone where armed forces are not allowed
almost no people or goods cross

parts.sample: The boundary at B is the Korean Demilitarized Zone, a strip about 4 km wide with fences and guard posts on each side where no armed forces may enter, and it stops almost all people and goods from crossing between North Korea and South Korea.

parts.label: C
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain why the boundary at C is often classed as an antecedent boundary.

rubric.point: Links the timing (drawn before large-scale settlement) to the type.
accept: drawn in 1881 along the Andes before many settlers lived there, so settlement grew up later
remote high mountains had few settlers when the line was agreed

parts.sample: It is called antecedent because Chile and Argentina agreed in 1881 that it would follow the high peaks of the Andes, before many settlers lived in that remote land, so settlement grew up on each side after the line was drawn.

parts.label: D
parts.demand: Give the specific meaning of the term, in your own words, not an example of it.

rubric.point: Says it is the sea up to 200 nautical miles from a state's coast where that state controls the resources.
accept: sea up to 200 nautical miles from the coast
the coastal state has rights to fish, oil, gas and minerals

parts.sample: An exclusive economic zone is the sea up to 200 nautical miles from a state's coast, where that state has the rights to the fish, oil, gas and other resources, though other states' ships may still sail through it.

parts.label: E
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain one reason several states claim islands and reefs in the sea at D.

rubric.point: Links control of the islands to rights over surrounding waters and their resources (or to control of shipping routes).
accept: islands can bring rights to the waters around them, so fish, oil and gas

parts.sample: Because control of land at sea can bring rights to the waters around it under the law of the sea, states claim the islands at D to gain fishing grounds and possible oil and gas, which is why China, Viet Nam, the Philippines and others make overlapping claims.

parts.label: F
parts.demand: Say how or why, with every link of the chain: a cause, then because or so, then its effect, tied to the place or data asked about.
parts.prompt: Explain how the boundary at B affects migration between the two states it separates.

rubric.point: Links the closed boundary to blocked or rerouted migration (an intervening obstacle).
accept: an intervening obstacle, so very few people cross directly
people who leave take long routes through other states

parts.sample: The boundary at B is an intervening obstacle: because guards, fences and mines block crossing, very few people can migrate directly from North Korea to South Korea, so most who leave take a long route through China instead.

parts.label: G
parts.demand: State the degree first (to a high, moderate or low degree), then explain why with evidence.
parts.prompt: Explain the degree to which a world map like this one can show how a boundary affects daily life at the local scale.

rubric.point: States a degree, then explains what the world map can and cannot show at the local scale.
accept: to a small degree: it shows where boundaries are, not local crossings or daily life
local data such as fieldwork or a large-scale map would be needed

parts.sample: To a small degree: the map shows where each boundary lies at the global scale, but it cannot show local details such as crossing points, markets or families split by the line, so fieldwork or a large-scale map would be needed to see daily life.
